headline: The preprint website arXiv has limited each person to two new submissions a month because a surge in papers, partly driven by AI tools, is overwhelming its volunteer moderators.
score_reason: Lowered from 6: the cap began on 1 Oct 2026 and we carried it on 2 Oct; today's report adds arXiv's figures and reasons but no new decision.
importance_line: Researchers who post on arXiv, especially AI authors, must now ration their submissions, and the site's own figures show how fast AI-assisted publishing is straining open sharing of papers, but the cap is described as temporary and the report does not say how much of the surge is AI-written.
summary: The Decoder reports that arXiv, the free website where researchers post papers before formal review, has limited each person to two new submissions a month since 1 Oct 2026, the cap we first carried on 2 Oct 2026 from Startup Fortune. New here are arXiv's numbers and reasons: monthly submissions rose from 20,569 in September 2024 to 40,363 in September 2026, and Thomas Dietterich, chair of its Editorial Advisory Council, says a small share of authors send many low-quality papers and use up a disproportionate part of its volunteer moderators' time, while arXiv calls the cap a temporary fix until its moderation tools can scale.
notes: Read in full from the main session's fulltext copy. Older event (cap in force 1 Oct 2026) re-reported on 11 Oct 2026; our 2 Oct 2026 edition carried it (Startup Fortune, score 6) and the 6 Oct edition carried New Scientist's follow-on. Kept at 5 because the report adds arXiv's own numbers and reasons; the duplicate check against the 14 earlier reports should decide whether it prints.
